It's interesting to note that I was one of the more hostile people
towards Meddling when it first came out; I remain hostile to its
existence. I don't think people properly made the attempt to use the
card because of its nature of turning casual games into "not fun" for at
least two players; the person playing the Meddling deck, and the poor
bugger who's getting nailed by it.

I don't think it's a broken game-winner, by a long shot; there are
plenty of other strategies that are more consistent game-winners. But I
do think it was a bad direction to head, as it focused almost entirely
on denial of a basic resource.

> idea. Sadly, all recent major developments in the great game have IMO

> the old players have been ducking out of the game, generally with

Allow me to agree with this.

I effectively retired when Black Hand was released... and while Gehenna
was in playtest, and was actively ruining games in our group. I decided
then to stop purchasing cards, as I just didn't see the point of
attempting to play a game that could be so easily disrupted by a simple
deck (the 1- or 2-cap Computer Hacking deck, chock full of Gehenna
events). As it turned out, such a deck DID do fairly well in a number
of outings (Stefan Ferenci resoundingly making the finals of the 2004
LCQ with a similar deck was my own personal experience, but I know there
were plenty of others), but the sheer table hate it tended to generate
actually discouraged widespread use. Very few people like to play a
game where their deck is reviled from turn one, and targetted even more
afterwards... so even among people where social pressure should never
take its toll, it does in a very subtle way.

While social pressure prevented Gehenna events from seeing significant
play at first, I never particularly regretted my decision, as the #2
factor suddenly came into play after I had stopped for awhile: Time.

The game remains too much of a time investment. To be required to set
aside an entire day on the weekend to play only 3 or 4 games, in an
increasingly randomized environment, is just not my cup of tea anymore.
Nor is being forced to spend all my time table-talking and dealing just
to get somewhere. At one point in time I was happy to do this; I found
I no longer had the patience, and I have little patience to pick the
game up again.

I certainly miss the people I used to see on a regular basis, especially
while traveling. But, overall, I simply can't justify devoting the time
expenditure to V:TES anymore, and it's somewhat amusing that it took
taking a break from the game to realize how much of a time expenditure
it really was.

> deck". Also, please note that I actually believe the old players could
> mostly have put up with any one or two of the factors on my list. Just
> not all of them.

I feel the randomization of the game has largely continued, and it is
surely a bad thing. Tupdog should have been caught and corrected in
playtest; any idiot can collect the cards, put a basic Tupdog deck
together, and create havoc at a table, whether or not they win. Not
good for retaining those of us who rather enjoyed being able to _play_
our decks.

The Imbued actually strike me as a very well put-together expansion
taken in their own perspective, but now the Gehenna Event problem that I
was afraid of so long ago has finally come home to roost -- the most
effective deck with Imbued is the "Screw Vampires" version. More
randomized disruption, based entirely on whether an Imbued deck is at
your table. Again, not good. I think the Imbued could have added a
great deal to the game if the Events were not available.

So, after all this, I haven't purchased a single box of the Black Hand
sets or later, and I don't intend to at this time. For one, the
financial barrier to re-entry for me (even if some of the other problems
were corrected) is simply too high. (Note that I don't consider this
financial barrier to be one that anyone else possesses -- I just know
that my own approach to the game would compel me to provide myself ALL
the options available, and as such it would be a LOT of money to go back
and pick up all the sets inbetween. I have better things to do with
that money now, and more time to do it in.)

I never really made a big public deal of things when I made my decision,
because I truly do hate the "I'm quitting the game, convince me to stay"
sort of post that we saw for a long time both after WW took over, as
well as the ones in relation to the card back and art changes...
especially when it was followed up 3 months later by the same poster
commenting "Oops, I changed my mind". But, as it turns out, I never did
change my mind, so for those few of you who were wondering, well, now
you know. :)

I certainly wish the existing players good luck, and hope that the game
can be encouraged to flourish in a more effective fashion -- shortening
the play time without sacrificing the rich strategy, for example. But
it must continue to do so without me.

- --
Derek

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <w5SdnZcpgPKacBDZ...@giganews.com>, Derek Ray

<lor...@yahoo.com> writes:
>The Imbued actually strike me as a very well put-together expansion
>taken in their own perspective, but now the Gehenna Event problem that I
>was afraid of so long ago has finally come home to roost -- the most
>effective deck with Imbued is the "Screw Vampires" version. More
>randomized disruption, based entirely on whether an Imbued deck is at
>your table. Again, not good. I think the Imbued could have added a
>great deal to the game if the Events were not available.

It's one of the reasons I dislike some of the Events so much. Some of
them are great, well-balanced and interesting. They empower other
strategies, providing versatility that wasn't available before, or are
otherwise fun.

A good example, for me, is The Unmasking. +1 intercept for allies.
Yes, it's more powerful with Imbued than it was before - you could block
the allies being brought out, for example, if you were worried. Of the
more recent Event cards, there are some similarly good cards, too.
Anthelios empowers strategies, and may be too good, but is available to
everyone so it sort of balances out. Port Authority is a mild denial
strategy, but it's quite mild with it, so doesn't detract from fun so
much - it's no worse than, say, Camarilla Threat.

The problems are that there are cards which can destroy a deck, just
randomly. The thing is, LSJ presumably knows they can destroy decks -
which is why some of them are banned in Storyline tournaments. For
example, a Camarilla voting deck, using the First Tradition, Parity
Shift, Protect Thine Own is killed by Fall of the Camarilla. Ditto, an
Anathema/Alastor/Archon deck. Or any Red List Trophy deck - I can't
generate Red List vampires without my titles!

I am no less screwed if this happens in a non-Storyline tournament, and
for a deck that has a modus operandi of "Screw other decks on the
table", it's not hard for them to include it. Similarly, Fall of the
Sabbat. Similarly, Recalled to the Founder.

There's no built-in way for me to fight these cards. So I have to
include counters to them, most of which only work when the card is
played. So I have to have enough of the counter in my deck to have one
in hand by the time the worst cards are played.

Now, this may be fine but... If we assume that many decks do not need
Events, I will need all the defences I used to have. Any deck, pre-
Events, will have whatever defence it needs - combat defence, politics,
pool gain, bounce, rush, whatever. So now I have to pull a whole bunch
of those cards to stop myself being screwed by Events. So even when I
don't see Events, those events are stopping me playing my game.
Emergency Preparations is entirely pointless to a mid-cap deck (or
smaller) if it's not seen. Not to Be has no alternative use. So I have
to jettison some of the defence I need against every other deck in the
deck and put in defence against cards I won't see that often - but when
they do, they destroy a deck.

Note: if they don't destroy single clan, or sect-focused, decks, they
would not need to be banned in Storyline tournaments.

What's the problem here? They stop me playing my game. Not because I
was bad. That's fine. If you torporize all my vampires, that's fine.
I didn't include rush defence, and it happens over multiple turns. If I
get killed by Fall of the Camarilla, that's not because I failed on a
number of levels. It's not like normal vote defence, where I can fight
tooth and nail on every single vote, even if it falls flat. I just get
screwed. And a deck employing it, like the Imbued screw vampires deck,
doesn't even have to care significantly if it pulls it off. It just
wants to screw vampires.

It stops me playing my game - and for what benefit to V:TES as a whole?
Even if you or I do or don't like Protect Thine Own, it's not reasonable
to tell a player using it that a deck can simply stop them using it by
luck. For the rest of the game. Entirely. It's not one card for a
short period of time, like Delaying Tactics or Vox Domini. It's not one
card giving everyone else extra power for a long period of time, like
Vox Senis. It stops me outright, for the rest of the game, unless
you're ousted.

Ditto, a variety of other Event cards - but also Meddling of Semsith. I
get stopped from playing my game, but it's entirely random whether it
happens or not. It doesn't flow from basic game mechanics that have
been there since 1994, like whether you rushed my minion or not. It's
just "Did players include the card that says 'Screw minion phase actions
for the rest of the game'?"

Different tangent: Brinksmanship. Brinksmanship actively penalises me
playing my game. The more cards I play, the closer I am to dying. This
randomly penalizes players choosing to play a 60 card deck, also. Are
60 decks inherently more powerful than 90 card decks? They may be less
clumpy (due to randomness being slightly less likely to screw you), but
I don't see that they're hugely more powerful and stomping on everyone.
Do they need to be screwed? If yes, that should be addressed. If no,
why does this card need to disproportionately screw their game?

Again, it suddenly stops me playing my game.

Yes, of course, I can include vote defence. And people do! But
including vote defence does not mean you will be able to defend against
specific votes. They might be called cross-table when you're tapped
out. And if I play Vox Domini to fail that vote, I can't play Not to Be
to stop your Event card that turn. Great. Everyone, I think, knows
that including defence in a deck does not guarantee anything and that
it's largely a way of pushing away a given strategy, rather than a
guarantee of killing it dead. For example, if I have 4-6 Delaying
Tactics in a reasonably-crated deck, on average I will be able to have
more political influence and survive longer against a political deck -
but that doesn't mean I'll be able to fail any given vote, due to the
randomness of V:TES. A well-played political deck knows that I can't
have an infinite amount of Delaying Tactics - and even in a Twister
deck, it would be able to see what's going on. So I can defend against
politics, but defending against Brinksmanship or Meddling *specifically*
is pretty much a no-go - I may not have drawn it.

And being stopped from playing my game by another player including a
handful of cards, which I can't predict, isn't fun. It's just simply
not fun. Recalled to the Founder does not add to fun in V:TES. Anarch
Revolt was not fun; it forced every other deck on the table to stop
playing their own game in order to stop the entire table falling apart.
This is: a) not fun and b) stops me playing my game.

When this is fun is with decks like Nergal. Every single player knows
in advance that the final will be different. They know that the Nergal
deck will be powerful. Even if they haven't looked at the deck (as was
their right), anyone thinking for more than 0.0003 of a second would
realise "Hey, they set it up to be bled by 4 people at once, so maybe
they made the deck powerful to cope!" But that *is* fun. It's a new
strategy. It doesn't entirely screw my deck, it's just that Nergal is
very good. The weirdness - I can know about that in advance. It's not
like someone just pulled the Nergal deck out from nowhere, completely
changing the rules of the game at random. I know in advance. I come
prepared. I get a new and different challenge. That is, or at least
can be, fun.

Having my deck completely shot down because another player played Events
or votes that say "Screw other decks, without any downside to themself"
is not fun. It's random unfun.

Random unfun is not good for the game.

But you can argue that there's no problems with this, because social
pressures will just stop people playing the unfun deck. A few points
here:

1) Anarch Revolt should not have been changed if this is a winning
argument.

2) Anarch Revolt was NOT stopped by social pressures.

3) Anarch Revolt decks were some of the most unfun decks in the game,
guaranteed to get many groans when seen.

4) Social pressure against specific decks or specific cards is just as
bad as xCL players using social pressures to exclude stealth-
bleed cheese because it breaks their game. If it's bad there -
which it is - it's bad here.

If a player has a deck that they like playing, they shouldn't be
pressured into not playing it by social factors. Game-based factors,
such as the deck being difficult, untenable, too slow, possible
backfiring, a random crapshoot for them (as to who they sit next to,
say), and so on, prevent a deck being a sensible choice. Social
pressures and table hate simply cause aggravation.

--
James Coupe

unless the game is being pretty static. And whether your deck can
break out of a static gamestate is dependent primarily upon its
construction. I used to be REALLY opposed to time outs, because I felt
they were antithetical to playing at all. Most of the time IME it
would not be table talk, but 3 intercept decks on the same table, which
pretty much guarantees a timeout.

My solution has been to include LOTS of stealth (or LOTS of combat)
into whatever I'm playing. If I don't have a way to break static, I
ASSUME the deck will reach time more than I'd like and I fix it or I
disassemble it. This way, I have some control over a static
environment, instead of feeling cheated by not being allowed to finish
my game.

My point is, either way, if you hate table-talk OR static environments,
it's the same cure. Play !Malk bleed, for example, and use Elder
Impersonation. Regardless of environment, regardless of table-talkers,
it's just not a deck that gets timed out easily.

Y'know, having played with quite a few events myself in the past few
months, I really feel a need to interject here. The idea that there's
somehow no downside to playing with a ton of Events (under any
circumstance) is just wrong:

a) You can't use your discard phases for the normal cycling of cards.
When you have crap in your hand you have to flush it some other way,
like The Barrens or Dreams of the Sphinx. Nearly all (good) flush
tech/hand size increase can be contested, too.

b) You can't always play the event you want, when you want. Most of the
severely disabling events require other events in play. This requires
you to pack multiple events and some way of ensuring that the events
come into your hand in a playable order, either by storing them for
later somehow or playing with multiples of the "starter" events. Cards
like Storage Annex work, but compete with valuable master space against
the flush tech.

c) If you pack more than a few into your deck, you're likely to see
several in your hand at once, where they will sit for several turns
waiting to be played one at a time, further exacerbating the loss of
discard phases actions by effectively reducing your hand size.

d) If you want a particular event to have any likelihood of going off
you need multiples of that event and/or Fortschritt Library, further
exacerbating the loss of discard phase actions since you can't play the
extras when you draw them. You have to discard them somehow to keep
drawing into the rest of your deck.

e) Most of the severely disabling events also have hefty do not replace
clauses on them, again exacerbating the need for flush tech. You can
get around this with Visit from the Capuchin, but again, this competes
with the flush tech space.

Dealing with all these issues is difficult under the best of
circumstances.

None of this of course says anything about how fun they are/aren't to
play with or against, which is largely a matter of taste and partly a
matter of familiarity. Nor does it say much about the "randomness" it
introduces to the table, which is mostly dependent on familiarity and
annoyance level (personally, I'm killed more by poor seating and/or
someone able to take advantage of my hand depletion than table hate).

> the Camarilla, 6 is more realistic. You can cycle 20-30 cards in that

By the Temptation of Greater Power standard you describe, you have 2 times
around the table to cycle into your Emergency Preparations after the first
Gehenna card lands on the table. Fall of the Camarilla could come exactly
two turns after that, and you have no real reason to expect it before at
least one Gehenna card enters play. You have one time around the table
after a Justicar is influenced into play (or voted into play) before ToGP
can be played. Not that much of an improvement. ("Realistically", you
probably have several turns after a Justicar enters play before ToGP gets
played - does that really help you that much in getting your hypothetical
Sudden Reversal?)

But the real point, I think, is that Sudden Reversal is even more
general-purpose a defense than Emergency Preparations, and even so, Sudden
Reversal isn't considered a really reliable defense against Temptation of
Greater Power. I think this is because planning on a defense versus other
players' offense, in many games (but perhaps especially VTES), is based on
what you expect to see and what you expect to be dangerous to you. In a
game like VTES, where the universe of possible threats continues to expand,
but your hand size, library size, and starting pool do not, planning to
directly defend against every likely threat becomes less and less feasible
over time.

That is, when the universe of "things to defend against" is "bleed",
"votes", and "combat", it is relatively feasible to include some defensive
measures in your own deck to deal with those threats. When the threats to
consider also include, say, "Smiling Jack", "Anarch Revolt",
"Brinksmanship", "Temptation of Greater Power", "Spirit Marionette", "Mind
Rape", "Gehenna events", and "all-allies Imbued decks", defense becomes less
possible. And the game evolves in a direction where offense trumps defense,
because no one can include defenses against everything that harms them. And
that leads toward a rock-paper-scissors environment, because some offensive
trumps beat others.

That, I think, is why some people are overwhelmed by or unhappy with Gehenna
events, Imbued decks, and the general addition of new mechanics (not
counterable by existing cards/strategies) to the game over time. The game
really *does* get more unwieldy, less manageable, and less comprehensible as
its universe of cards and their effects expands.

Josh

For what it's worth - though that's probably not much at this point - the

brokenness of Gehenna. The Gehenna events changed several times during
playtest, and were MUCH worse at the start (replaced immediately, stayed in

prophetic now:

"On the set as a whole, we've come back to the thing we're most concerned

could actually drive a significant proportion of the playerbase out of the
game because they can alter the game environment *so* much from the flavor
and texture of the "traditional" VTES game. Think about all the people who
don't enjoy heavy-Anarch-Revolt games, and then consider how much more the

not-broken-enough-to-scare-people-out-of-the-game. It would also be useful,

> for a equipment heavy deck. Another question: If your deck doesn't
> vote, how many card slots are you willing to sacrifice on vote defence?
> My guess is not alot, so your leaving the door open for another
> strategy anyway, how are events any different?

Events are different because they have a universal effect on every player
all the time, while votes are transient effects much like bleed cards (or
other action cards). Isn't that pretty obvious? Their impact is simply far
greater per card than almost anything else in the game.

> If YOU as a deck
> designer see tham as a significant threat, is it unreasonable to ask
> you to dedicate some of your deck to defend against them?. As far as
> the "rock, paper, scissors" environment goes, what is wrong with
> offence beating defence?

Well, it's not that offense shouldn't beat defense, but that defense
shouldn't get monotonically less effective over time. It's fine for offense
to beat defense: that's how pool gets lost, victory points get scored, and
games end. But if offense *always* beats defense, all the time, then
there's not much point in playing defense at all, is there?

> I can't agree with you dude, the defences remain the same, it's just
> the assault that differs. As far as diveristy goes, don't we as players
> want options? To slam WW or anyone else for thier choices just seems
> wrong to me. Yes they have added more rules with NoR, but dosn't every
> expansion of any game? Expansion= more options, simple as that,
> otherwise it wouldn't be an expansion, just a re-hash of previously
> covered ground.

I don't think that's accurate. I think that's how it probably *should* be -
that defenses remain the same but the assault differs - but I don't think it
has been. That's exactly the issue here: Events cannot be defended against
or dealt with through the same cards and methods as previous "bad things"
that other players could do to you.

No, every expansion of every game doesn't *have* to add new rules. You can
do plenty of things with card text without expanding the basic ruleset.
That's pretty much what was done with Sabbat War, Final Nights, and Black
Hand, for example.

> Should we have 10 cards that say "I bleed you for 1" or 10 cards that
> say "I bleed you for one and ........?
> I'll go for option number two, sounds more interesting to me :)

Well, I certainly agree with *that*. But there's a pretty big difference
between a new bleed card - even one with an interesting additional effect,
even if it's a *strong* effect - and a new cardtype that affects every
subsequent card played in the game and cannot be blocked as an action, isn't
a master card, and can't be removed (for the most part) once in play.

To me, a big part of the reason Events don't fit well into the framework of
VTES is that they are large-effect cards. VTES was built on a framework of
relatively small-effect cards that add up to large effects in combination or
over the play of many cards over multiple turns. That's why immediate
replacement of cards was such a crucial mechanic in the game - it makes
those small-effect cards playable because you can play another small-effect
card right away; you don't have to always get the most bang for your buck as
you would in games with slower, more limited card replacement. Meanwhile,
the largest-effect cards in the original game of VTES are all the most
powerful ones, and a rather substantial number of them later received errata
to reduce their strength: Wake with Evening's Freshness, Temptation of
Greater Power, Fifth Tradition: Hospitality, Majesty, et cetera. But none
of those really even compare to the magnitude of effect that some of the
Gehenna cards have.

Josh

Well... Much like Derek, never thought it would need a public
announcement or something like that just to see if someone convinces me
of the contrary, but I also quit buying V:tES cards.

Most of the reasons for this decision are vastly different from what
has been mentioned so far though. None of them are directly related to
the game design. I played a little bit of it as soon as Dark Sovereigns
came here, then quit because I couldn't find anyone else who played
except for this guy who showed me the game, and came back to it after
moving to Sao Paulo a year or so before Camarilla Edition.

Now it just happens that I'm not that thrilled anymore. Half of the fun
for me is the deckbuilding part and I don't have time to come up with a
new deck a week (as Josh). I also don't want to devote a whole day or
night to play only 2 or 3 games anymore (as Derek). When I got back to
the game, it seemed a good alternative to roleplaying since it didn't
require the same amount of preparation a storytelling session implies.
After a few years playing V:tES, I think I was wrong: to maintain a
collection in good shape and to build/disassemble decks takes a lot of
time too. Not to mention trading, which is an essential part of the
whole experience if you don't have a lot of money to spend in boxes.

It also didn't help that I got hooked by Requiem. I know people will
get offended by this, but to me, Requiem is Masquerade without the fat,
and it's been hard for me to relate to old WoD as I used to. Right, I
know many of you never got to VTES from the roleplaying hobby, but I
did - as most people here also did. Background is essential for me to
have enjoyment playing VTES.

Logistical problems also don't help. We still don't have NoR material
around here. It's not WW's fault, just some boring customs officials'
strike that kept the pre-release boxes in Miami to this date. I could
import it, but it would cost me money that I've already spent in books
just going to the closest store (books are free of taxes in here). Call
me lazy, but no matter how easy it is to contact AllStar or
TheLasombra, it gets boring when you have to do this all the time just
to keep in touch and updated with something that is just a hobby. When
you have to choose between buying a roleplaying book right now - that
you can keep and re-read for the rest of your life, even if you don't
use it in a game - and importing a booster box via the internet - that
you can only effectively use if you go play and will take a week or two
to arrive - for financial and practical reasons, it's natural to go for
the book. At least for me.

The only thing I can say that is directly related to the game as it is
now is the frequency of expansions, but it's a minor thing, at least
for me.

While some play less because they miss the old friends who quit (like
Legbiter), I'm going for the exact opposite. I played VTES *despite*
the presence of some, specially some older players. These are people
that I wouldn't go to a bar with to have a beer and engage in idle
chatting, and this gets in the way after a few years. Roleplaying has
the advantage that you can just kick the troublesome ones out (if
you're the storyteller like I usually am) and just look for other
interested players - something you can't do when, say, you're playing a
VTES tournament.

I'm still playing, but in a pace that takes into account that I won't
move a single finger to build a deck or pack the ready ones and go out
to play unless it's the last thing I can do with my spare time. Reading
books (roleplaying ones or not), going to the movies or for dinner with
my wife, or simply having a good nap at saturday afternoon comes first.

Or better: watch the English Team suffer to beat Trinidad and Tobago or
support any team that plays against Argentina during the World Cup :)

Currently, you can get a game win with 2VPs, assuming no one else has 2
or more VPs in the game. So when you sit down at a 5 player game, you
can win assuming you can:

A) Oust your first prey.
B) Keep everyone else from getting more than 1 VP.

(A) is usually not that hard. (B) is harder, but certainly possible
through clever play and/or wheeling and dealing. But the end result is
that if you can oust 1 person and then play the table, you can win,
even if you are ousted in the end. Meaning that you kind of run out of
really solid incentive to oust your prey after getting 1VP.

you needed *3* VPs to get a "table win", everyone would have a lot more
incentive, to, ya know, oust their prey which would result in more
agressive play and less table dealing.

tournament in Northampton this last weekend with some certainly world
class players, and none of the two preliminary games I played in nor
the final involved any significant table talk or deals of any type.
Everyone just, ya know, tried to oust their prey...)

maneuver gets used a lot. If you maneuver away from a Grapple with
your gun, you often end up eating steel pie. And losing too much blood
- either through damage or rescues - kills the tiny pool gain you can
afford to pack, making you even more vulnerable to the usual problem of
light stealth + big bleed or vote from your predator.

Also annoying: Tremere. Just plain old vanilla Theft is bad, but I
seem to run into more than my share of Thelerity, which is a duel I
tend to lose. Ending up empty at the end of combat is not good, even
if the other guy goes down.

Opposing guns is also a problem, though not as big of one, as you at
least tend to see them coming. .44's are a very popular defensive
option.

Bottom line: rush combat needs to win combat. Losing more than a
little pretty much means you are done.

Also, POT weenies expect to lose weenies, and pot weenies in particular
are cheap enough to be disposable. CEL weenies are not cheap (minimum
of 3-cap for Sarah + 2 pool for the gun = 5 pool invested). So it's
much more important that combat go your way with CEL/guns.
(Additionally, losing gunners to torpor is a problem, 'cause if you let
them sit, someone else will diablerize them and often end up with a gun
of their own.)

CEL/guns generally, IME, wants to be as weenie as it can. There are
bigger cap variants, but they aren't usually rush. (Tories come
quickly to mind, either intercepting or voting.) My current CCGW
variant is Assamite based, but that doesn't actually make much of a cap
difference with the current pool of vampires there - it just lets me
use some Swallowed by the Night for stealth/more maneuvers.

> > defenses at all.

> was mostly accurate, except for the fact that, of the combat I expect
> to see, I expect a lot of it to be ANI combat, which is the natural
> trump for guns. I suspect our different perspectives come down mostly
> to metagame issues (although to be clear, I am talking about my
> tournament meta).

I like that CEL/guns makes another rush type relatively viable. I
don't see it as particularly overpowered - it has all the usual rush
problems (few masters = pool management problems, no bounce/intercept =
proactive defense, other combat trumps, etc.). In fact, in the CCGW
environment, it's often underpowered - I've brought handguns to an
artillery duel, and have all these pointless rush and S:CE hoser cards
to boot!

But man, I looked at the decklists for the NW Qualifier, and just
drooled, thinking what my gunners would have done there... It would
have been beautiful.

So, I guess I tend to agree that 'no combat defense' is an increasingly
reasonable option. And I guess CEL/guns is a part of that. But I
think it's really that there are just so many different viable ways to
get killed in combat these days. Yay!

Given that we just recently got Concealed Weapon 'fixed' to (IMO) great
effect, I wonder if now wouldn't be an OK time to 'fix' Wake too?

Current card:

Wake with Evening's Freshness
Reaction
Do not replace until your next untap phase.
Only usable by a tapped vampire. This reacting vampire can use reaction
cards and attempt to block as though untapped until the current action
is concluded.

'Fixed' card:

Wake with Evening's Freshness
Reaction
Thaumaturgy
tha: Only usable by a tapped vampire. This reacting vampire can use
reaction cards and attempt to block as though untapped until the
current action is concluded. Do not replace this card until your next
untap phase.
THA: As above, but this card is replaced immediately.

Yes, this would cause a major paradigm shift, but I suspect it might be
in a good direction. What do people use Wakes for? Blocking or
bouncing, pretty much.

A currently existing deck that uses Wakes for blocking could swap into
Forced Awakenings without a huge impact. You would probably want to be
a little more serious about blocking - to avoid the blood loss - but
that's about it.

A currently existing deck that uses Wakes for bouncing, OTOH, is going
to pay a big penalty at this point. And which decks bounce? That's
right, decks with Dominate and/or superior Auspex. Auspex decks will
suffer less - their bounce cards help them block as well - but now
they're going to be paying more to bounce. Dominate decks have a hard
choice: Forced Awakening means paying another blood to bounce; no
Forced Awakening means leaving minions untapped, which means either
less bleeding, or more blood lost to Freak Drive. And to me, weakening
Dominate is a big plus.

Additional plus: offense become stronger relative to defense = shorter
games.

Sure, it's also a gift to the Tremere, which they don't really need.
But I don't see it making them, like, way overpowered or anything.
They, of the Dominate using clans (Malks, Ventrue, Giovanni, Lasombra),
are the ones who, IMO, are least able to abuse Dominate anyway (no
stealth, not much multi-act), and increasing their intercept abilities
relative to other clans (by lowering other clans') might give them an
interesting new focus.

Anyway, begin discussion of how this suggestion is both 'broken' and
'wallpaper' now...

Alex

> > more common problem than what to do when you're ousted early.

> Exactly so.

If THIS is something you meant when you expressed dissatisfaction with
the direction of the game, then I fully agree. The tools exist to slow
down the game at least enough, and possibly too much. People may not
always use them, but they exist.

No new tools need to be made, unless they aren't readily usable with
the current tools. For example, if there were a reaction for vampires
which fails an action and forces combat (like Champion power from NoR),
I would be in favor should it require, say, cel+obf, but not if it
should require AUS or ANI.

Still, I've been upset about Bowl of Convergence, the advent of AUS
weenie decks as a tournament force, the ubiquity of intercept at every
table under almost every player's control, etc. I believe these things
are responsible for slowing or stopping the game far more than Meddling
of Semsith or most of the Gehenna events are.

Maybe your experience differs.

-- Brian
